title: Hartford Wash: Washing, Tracks, Maintenance (Outside)
kind: Performance at the Wadsworth Atheneum, Hartford, 1973
note: One of her Maintenance Art performances at the Wadsworth Atheneum, 1973 to 1974
story: In 1969, after the birth of her first child, Ukeles wrote her Manifesto for Maintenance Art, which argued that the daily work of cleaning, keeping and caring, done unseen and mostly by women, was as much art as anything shown in a gallery. In 1973 the Wadsworth Atheneum in Hartford let her put it into practice: she washed the plaza and steps outside the museum on her hands and knees, then the floors inside, during opening hours. The pictures show the work a museum depends on and does not exhibit.

spaces.tie: Mierle Laderman Ukeles, Hartford Wash, performance, 1973

title: Hartford Wash: Washing, Tracks, Maintenance (Outside)
kind: Performance at the Wadsworth Atheneum, Hartford, 1973

title: Museum Highlights: A Gallery Talk
kind: Performance at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, 1989
story: As Jane Castleton, an invented volunteer docent, Fraser led visitors through the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 1989. She praised the water fountain, the cafeteria and the toilets in the same gushing words a guide uses for the paintings, with lines taken from the museum's own guidebooks, annual reports and older writing on museums. The talk asks what a museum teaches its visitors besides art: manners, taste and the idea that culture improves those it lets in. Tate holds the video of the performance.

spaces.tie: Andrea Fraser, Museum Highlights: A Gallery Talk, performance, 1989

title: You’re Seeing Less Than Half the Picture
kind: Poster, 1989. Tate collection
story: The Guerrilla Girls formed in New York in 1985, after the Museum of Modern Art opened a survey of recent painting and sculpture with barely a dozen women among more than 160 artists. They work anonymously in gorilla masks, taking the names of dead women artists, and answer with counts: how many women and artists of colour museums and galleries show. This 1989 poster says it in one line, that a collection without them leaves out more than half the picture. Tate holds a set of their posters from these years.

title: Guerrilla Girls’ Code of Ethics for Art Museums
kind: Poster, 1990. Tate collection
story: By 1990 the Guerrilla Girls had spent five years posting statistics about who museums show. This poster turns to how museums behave, set out as a list of commandments addressed to the institutions themselves. Like their other posters it was pasted up in the streets of New York and later collected by the museums it addressed, Tate among them.

title: Guards
kind: Installation view, Artists Space, New York, 2015
note: A film made at the Art Institute of Chicago with museum guards who had served in the military or the police
credit: Courtesy the artist and Andrew Kreps, New York.
story: Steyerl made Guards in 2012 at the Art Institute of Chicago, filming two of the museum's guards, both of whom had served in the military or the police. In the galleries they describe how they would secure a room, where a threat would come from and how to clear it, as if the museum were a combat zone. The film sets the protection of art beside the training of people whose earlier jobs were violence, and asks what the calm of a museum rests on.

spaces.tie: Hito Steyerl, Guards, a film made with the museum’s guards, 2012

title: Guards
kind: Image from the video. KOW, Berlin

title: Is the Museum a Battlefield?
kind: Two-channel video installation. Collection of the Museo Reina Sofía, Madrid
story: Steyerl first gave this as a lecture at the 13th Istanbul Biennial in 2013. It follows a bullet casing found in Kurdistan, near where her friend Andrea Wolf was killed in 1998, back to the arms makers that produced such ammunition, and finds some of the same companies among the sponsors of art events and museums. The talk was turned into a two-channel video installation, which the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid now holds.

spaces.tie: Hito Steyerl, Is the Museum a Battlefield?, a lecture at the 13th Istanbul Biennial, 2013

title: Is the Museum a Battlefield?
kind: Two-channel video installation. Collection of the Museo Reina Sofía, Madrid

title: Duty Free Art
kind: Installation view, Artists Space, New York, 2015
note: A lecture given at Artists Space, New York, in March 2015, on freeports, where artworks worth millions are stored untaxed
story: Steyerl gave Duty Free Art as a lecture at Artists Space in New York in March 2015, during her exhibition there. It is about freeports, the bonded warehouses in places such as Geneva where art worth millions is stored untaxed and rarely seen, bought and sold without leaving the building. For Steyerl the freeport is the art world's offshore account, a museum with no public. The lecture was later shown as a video installation.

spaces.tie: Hito Steyerl, Duty Free Art, a lecture, 2015

title: Duty Free Art
kind: Installation view. KOW, Berlin

title: 5 weeks, 25 days, 175 hours
kind: The closed gallery, Chisenhale Gallery, London, 2016
note: For the length of the exhibition, 23 April to 29 May 2016, the gallery and office were closed and the staff were not working
credit: Images courtesy of the artist. Commissioned by Chisenhale Gallery. Photos by Andy Keate.
story: Chisenhale Gallery in London commissioned Eichhorn for 2016. She answered by closing it: for the five weeks of the exhibition, the gallery and its office stayed shut and the staff did not work, while being paid as usual. The title counts the working time they were given back. A symposium on work and its refusal opened the project, and the closed gate with its notice was all a visitor saw. The piece asked what a small public gallery runs on, and who pays for its constant activity.

spaces.tie: Maria Eichhorn, 5 weeks, 25 days, 175 hours, exhibition, 2016

title: 5 weeks, 25 days, 175 hours
kind: Sign on the gate, Chisenhale Gallery, London, 2016

title: Debtfair
kind: Installation view, Whitney Biennial, Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, 2017
credit: Occupy Museums. Installation view. Debtfair, 2017. Thirty artworks and interactive website. Courtesy the artists. Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, N.Y. Photograph by Ronald Amstutz
story: Occupy Museums grew out of Occupy Wall Street in 2011, taking its protest against debt and inequality into New York's museums. For the 2017 Whitney Biennial it showed Debtfair: the work of thirty artists set into the walls in groups by the kind of debt they carry, from student loans to mortgages and credit cards, with a website that gathered the stories of many more. Shown in a museum whose trustees include financiers, it asked who pays for an art career and who profits from it.

spaces.tie: Occupy Museums, Debtfair, in the Whitney Biennial, 2017

title: 2016 in Museums, Money, and Politics
kind: Print, 2018. Collection of the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
credit: Purchase, with funds from the Print Purchase Fund. © Thea Westreich Wagner, Ethan Wagner, and Andrea Fraser
story: For this work Fraser looked up the political donations made during the 2016 United States elections by the trustees of 128 American museums, and listed them, museum by museum, with the sums and the candidates and causes they went to. It was published as a book in 2018 and shown as prints and wall text. Set out in plain columns, the figures show how museum boards and political money overlap. The Whitney Museum, one of the museums listed, holds a set of the prints.

title: Protest at the Whitney Museum
kind: Banners in the lobby of the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, 5 April 2019
note: A protest over Warren Kanders, vice chair of the museum’s board
story: In November 2018 tear gas canisters made by Safariland, a company owned by the Whitney's vice chair, Warren Kanders, were reported to have been fired at migrants at the United States border with Mexico. Museum staff wrote an open letter, and Decolonize This Place led nine weeks of protest in the spring of 2019, with banners and marches in the museum's lobby. In July 2019 several artists asked to withdraw their work from that year's Biennial, and Kanders resigned from the board days later.

spaces.tie: Decolonize This Place, protest over the board’s vice chair Warren Kanders, 2019

title: Triple-Chaser
kind: Installation view, Whitney Biennial, Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, 2019
credit: Installation view of the Whitney Biennial 2019 (Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, May 17-September 22, 2019). Forensic Architecture, Triple-Chaser, 2019. Photograph by Ron Amstutz
story: Forensic Architecture, a research group based at Goldsmiths in London, made Triple-Chaser with Praxis Films for the 2019 Whitney Biennial. The film looks into the tear gas grenades made by Safariland, the company owned by the museum's vice chair Warren Kanders, and shows how the group trained software on synthetic images to find the canisters in footage from protests around the world. In July 2019 Forensic Architecture was among the artists who asked to withdraw from the Biennial; Kanders resigned days later.

spaces.tie: Forensic Architecture, Triple-Chaser, in the Whitney Biennial, 2019

title: Triple-Chaser
kind: Installation view, Whitney Biennial, Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, 2019
credit: Installation view of the Whitney Biennial 2019 (Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, May 17-September 22, 2019). Forensic Architecture, Triple-Chaser, 2019. Photograph by Ron Amstutz

title: Mass action at the British Museum
kind: The BP logo pulled apart in the Great Court of the British Museum, London, 23 April 2022
note: A protest against the museum’s sponsor, the oil company BP
credit: The giant logo is pulled apart. Photo by Ron Fassbender.
story: BP or not BP? is a group of actors and activists who began in 2012 by staging uninvited theatre against the oil company's sponsorship of the Royal Shakespeare Company and the British Museum. On 23 April 2022 it filled the museum's Great Court for a day of protest, ending with a giant BP logo pulled apart and the crowd singing. The museum's contract with BP ran out in 2023, and in December that year it signed a new ten-year agreement with the company worth £50 million.

spaces.tie: BP or not BP?, mass action against the sponsor BP, 2022

title: Mass action at the British Museum
kind: Performers lead the crowd in song, Great Court of the British Museum, London, 23 April 2022
credit: Performers lead the crowd in song. Photo by Kristian Buus.

title: Guerrilla Girls Review the Whitney
kind: Poster for the exhibition at The Clocktower, New York, 16 April to 17 May 1987. Tate collection
story: In the spring of 1987, while the Whitney Biennial was on, the Guerrilla Girls put on an exhibition of their own at The Clocktower, a city-owned space in lower Manhattan run by the Institute for Art and Urban Resources. It set out, in posters and figures, how few women and artists of colour the Whitney had shown in its Biennials and its collection. The poster gives the dates and the place, under a Guerrilla Girl in her mask.

spaces.tie: Guerrilla Girls, Guerrilla Girls Review the Whitney, poster, 1987

title: It’s Even Worse in Europe
kind: Poster, 1986. Tate collection
story: In their first years the Guerrilla Girls pasted posters at night on the walls of SoHo, then New York's gallery district, naming the museums, galleries and critics that showed or wrote about few women. This 1986 poster is one sentence long and signed, as they all were, as a public service message from the conscience of the art world. Whatever the figures in New York, it says, the museums of Europe were worse. Tate, one of those museums, later acquired it.

title: Etude pour La Lecture, 1923, This Drawing is for Sale, Paris
kind: Photograph, 1985. Tate collection
story: Since the late 1970s Louise Lawler has photographed other artists' work where it ends up: in museums, private collections, auction rooms and storage. Her pictures show that a work's meaning changes with where it hangs and who owns it. Here a framed study by Fernand Léger stands propped on other pictures beside a leather seat, and the title, which names the drawing and says it is for sale in Paris, turns a masterpiece into stock.

title: March 25, 1991
kind: Photograph, 1991. Tate collection
story: Lawler took this picture of one of Roy Lichtenstein's large interior paintings, a living room drawn in his comic-book line, with two shipping crates standing in front of it on a bare floor. Titled only with the date, it catches the painting between places, packed or about to be, the way most art spends much of its life. It belongs to the work Lawler has made since the late 1970s on how art is handled, moved, stored and sold.

title: Foreground
kind: Photograph, 1994. Tate collection
story: A stainless steel rabbit by Jeff Koons, one of the most expensive sculptures of its time, stands on a plinth in a private apartment, while the photograph gives most of its space to the kitchen beside it: a fridge, cupboards and a counter. Lawler photographs art in the homes of collectors as she does in museums, and lets the setting speak. The title asks what is in the foreground, the art or the life of the people who own it.

title: Grey Area
kind: Five painted plaster busts on wooden shelves, 1993. Tate collection
story: A year after Mining the Museum, in which he rearranged the collection of the Maryland Historical Society to show the history of slavery it had kept out of sight, Fred Wilson made Grey Area. It sets five casts of the bust of Nefertiti side by side, painted in steps from white to black. The original was dug up at Amarna by a German expedition in 1912 and is in Berlin, which Egypt has asked to return. Wilson's row asks how museums have decided who the ancient Egyptians were, and whose history they are telling.

title: Adjusted
note: Her first large exhibition in Germany, 11 October 2013 to 26 January 2014
credit: Images courtesy of the artist; Metro Pictures, New York; and Museum Ludwig, Cologne
kind: Installation view, Museum Ludwig, Cologne, 2013
story: Museum Ludwig gave Lawler her first large exhibition in Germany, curated by Philipp Kaiser. Rather than keeping to one suite of rooms, about 80 of her photographs were placed through the whole building, among the museum's own collection, so that her pictures of art in other museums, collections and auction rooms met the works on the walls beside them. She also made ten new tracings, outlines of her earlier photographs that look like pages of a colouring book, and two stretches, photographs printed on vinyl and pulled to fit the wall even where that distorts them.

spaces.tie: Louise Lawler, Adjusted, exhibition, 2013 to 2014

title: Shapolsky et al. Manhattan Real Estate Holdings, a Real-Time Social System, as of May 1, 1971
kind: Six of the photograph and text panels, 1971, in the collection of the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
credit: Purchased jointly by the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York with funds from the Director's Discretionary Fund and the Painting and Sculpture Committee, and the Fundació Museu d'Art Contemporani de Barcelona. © Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York / VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn
story: Hans Haacke searched New York's public records and traced the property dealings of the landlord Harry Shapolsky from 1951 to 1971. He set out 146 photographs of Manhattan apartment buildings beside maps and typed sheets on each building's owners. The work was made for his solo show at the Guggenheim Museum in spring 1971. The museum cancelled the show six weeks before the opening and fired the curator, Edward F. Fry, who had backed the work.

title: Musée Précaire Albinet
kind: Visitors in front of a painting on loan in the exhibition room of the temporary museum, Cité Albinet, Aubervilliers, 2004
story: Thomas Hirschhorn built a temporary museum with residents at the foot of the Cité Albinet housing block in Aubervilliers, north of Paris, at the invitation of Les Laboratoires d'Aubervilliers. From 19 April to 14 June 2004 it showed original works lent by the Centre Pompidou and the Fonds National d'Art Contemporain, in eight exhibitions that ran from Duchamp and Malevich to Warhol. The Centre Pompidou first trained residents in art handling and security. The site also had a library and a snack bar run by local women.

title: Tatlin's Whisper #5
kind: The two riders and the crowd during the performance, Tate Modern, London, 2008
story: In 2008 Tania Bruguera sent two mounted police officers in uniform onto the Turbine Hall bridge at Tate Modern in London, during the programme UBS Openings: Live The Living Currency, curated by Pierre Bal-Blanc. The performance was not announced to the visitors. The officers used crowd control techniques on them. One horse cornered the audience, the crowd split into two groups, and the riders pushed the groups together again as their circle shrank. Most visitors did what the officers told them to do.

spaces.tie: Tania Bruguera, Tatlin's Whisper #5, unannounced performance with mounted police in the Turbine Hall, 2008

title: Museum Songspiel: The Netherlands 20XX
kind: The film on screen, 2011: the chorus of attendants in Van Abbemuseum shirts
story: Chto Delat made the film in 2011, directed by Olga Egorova, known as Tsaplya, with music by Mikhail Krutik. It is set in a future Netherlands that has banned all immigrants. A guard at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven finds a group of immigrants hiding in a glass display case. A choir of museum attendants sings the score. At the end the museum director tells a journalist that the museum had hired the group as actors for a performance. The Van Abbemuseum acquired the film the same year.

spaces.tie: Chto Delat, Museum Songspiel: The Netherlands 20XX, film set in the museum and held in its collection, 2011

title: The Business Behind Art Knows the Art of the Koch Brothers
kind: Installation of three framed photographs and collaged hundred dollar bills, Paula Cooper Gallery, New York, 2014
story: On 9 September 2014 the Metropolitan Museum of Art dedicated its rebuilt Fifth Avenue plaza and named it after David H. Koch, a trustee who paid the 65 million dollar cost. Hans Haacke showed the installation at Paula Cooper Gallery in New York from 25 October to 13 December 2014. Two photographs show the new fountains, marked David H. Koch Plaza in gold. A third shows a banner on the museum's facade printed with the Met leaflet that the title quotes. Oversized hundred dollar bills pour from the frames.

spaces.tie: Hans Haacke, The Business Behind Art Knows the Art of the Koch Brothers, installation about the David H. Koch Plaza, 2014

title: Bakunin's Barricade
kind: The barricade in the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, 2020, with works from the museum's collection by Kazimir Malevich and Nan Goldin
story: In 2015 Ahmet Öğüt built a barricade in the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven and hung paintings from the museum's collection on it. The idea came from Mikhail Bakunin's unrealised plan of 1849 in Dresden. A contract written with the lawyer Marianne Korpershoek lets protesters ask to borrow the work. The Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam signed it five years later. In June 2024 cultural workers asked for the barricade to protect student protests over Gaza. The museum offered reproductions. In October 2024 Öğüt demanded that the Stedelijk take his work off display.

title: The Natural History Museum
kind: Display case labelled The David H. Koch Dinosaur Wing, at the American Alliance of Museums convention, Atlanta, 2015
note: The Natural History Museum is the collective's own project, not the New York museum it copies.
story: The art collective Not An Alternative launched The Natural History Museum in 2014 as a travelling museum of its own. From 15 to 19 May 2015 it took the largest exhibitor space at the American Alliance of Museums convention in Atlanta, where 7,000 museum staff from 60 countries met. There it rebuilt displays from the American Museum of Natural History in New York and added what that museum left out: facts about David H. Koch, its board member and biggest sponsor.

spaces.tie: Not An Alternative, The Natural History Museum, rebuilt displays naming the board member David H. Koch, 2015

title: No River to Cross
kind: The Open Letter, three framed handwritten sheets, at Kunstverein München, 2021
credit: Installation views: Bea Schlingelhoff, No River to Cross, Kunstverein München, 2021. Courtesy the artist and Kunstverein München e.V.; photos: Constanza Meléndez.
story: For her exhibition at Kunstverein München from 11 September to 21 November 2021, Bea Schlingelhoff studied how the association had worked with the Nazi regime. By 1936 it had barred people it called non-Aryans from membership. Part of the 1937 exhibition Degenerate Art was held in the building it moved into in 1953. She wrote an amendment to the bylaws in which the Kunstverein apologises for that cooperation and commits itself to non-discrimination. The proposal went to a vote of its nearly 1,300 members.

spaces.tie: Bea Schlingelhoff, No River to Cross, exhibition and proposed amendment to the bylaws, 2021
